artifacts.body:
# Draft: telling families about the cooked plates

This is a working draft for your review. Nothing has been posted, sent, or changed on any listing.

The point of this is simple. People searching "Harborview" see sushi and some assume there is nothing for a child or an adult who does not eat raw fish. One sentence in your listing descriptions, two clear photos, and one habit at the table fixes that.

---

## 1. The one line for your listings

**Short version (use where space is tight):**

> Sushi, plus cooked plates like chicken teriyaki, panko chicken katsu, and tempura for anyone who does not eat raw fish.

**Longer version (use where the field allows a full paragraph):**

> Harborview serves sushi in Harbor Point, along with cooked Japanese plates for guests who do not eat raw fish, including chicken teriyaki, panko chicken katsu, and tempura. Families and larger groups are welcome, and we can put a cooked plate in front of anyone at the table.

Before this goes anywhere, confirm the three dish names match how they read on your menu. If a plate is listed differently, use your exact menu wording instead.

---

## 2. Where the line goes

| Place | Field | Which version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Google Business Profile | Business description | Longer |
| Yelp | Business description / "About" | Longer |
| TripAdvisor | Description | Longer |
| DoorDash store description | Store or menu header text | Short |

Add the line to the existing description rather than replacing everything already written there.

---

## 3. Photo shot list

Two photos, taken in daylight near a window, no flash.

1. **Chicken teriyaki plate** as it is actually served, full plate in frame, shot from slightly above.
2. **Panko chicken katsu plate** the same way, so the panko crust is visible.

For both: clean plate rim, wipe the table, no clutter or hands in frame, no filters. Take three or four frames of each and keep the clearest one.

Where they go:
- Google Business Profile photos, food category
- The matching DoorDash menu items, so the cooked plates are not the only items without a picture

---

## 4. What servers say when a family is seated

One sentence, said once, while handing over menus:

> "If anyone is not eating raw fish tonight, we have chicken teriyaki, chicken katsu, and tempura."

Guidance for the team:
- Say it when children are at the table or when a guest hesitates over the menu.
- Say it once. If nobody responds, move on.
- Do not push it on guests who order sushi right away.

---

## 5. Checking whether it worked

Give it three to four weeks, then look at two things:

- Are cooked plates showing up more often in delivery orders and on table checks?
- Are servers reporting that guests mention seeing the cooked plates online?

If nothing moves, the next step is photos of the cooked plates on the website, not more listing text.

---

finds.rationale: Three separate hosts, captured on different days, carry three different public names. A business name is a durable field, not a momentary availability state, so open-or-shut does not bear on this claim; both platform captures fall inside posted trading hours in any case. Both Toast captures were fetched 2026-08-02T13:28:26Z, which is 6:28 AM Sunday local in America/Los_Angeles and before opening, so I make no claim about anything on that page being unavailable or broken — only about the durable text it displays.

# $35 Sushi & Sashimi Combo — rollout draft

Draft only. Nothing below has been posted, uploaded, printed, or sent.

## 1. The photo

One photo does all the work here, so shoot it once and use it everywhere.

- Plate the combo exactly as a guest would receive it.
- Shoot at the sushi bar during daylight, before service, with the house lights off if daylight is strong enough.
- Camera slightly above the plate, about a 45-degree angle, phone is fine.
- Wipe the bar surface and remove menus, condiment bottles, and receipts from the frame.
- Take 8 to 10 frames, pick one, and keep the original file. Do not crop it square before saving.

Use this same image on the website, Google Business Profile, and Yelp so the dish is recognizable across all three.

## 2. Menu page on harborview.example.com

Place the photo and the two lines below at the top of the menu page, above the existing menu sections.

> **Sushi & Sashimi Combo — $35**
> Chef's selection from the sushi bar.

If you want a longer line naming the pieces or cuts included, send me that detail and I will add it. The block works as written without it.

## 3. Table card for sushi-bar seats

One small card per sushi-bar seat, printed one-sided.

> **Sushi & Sashimi Combo**
> **$35**
> Ask your server or the sushi chef.

Keep the card small enough to sit flat next to the chopstick rest without crowding the setting.

## 4. Photo uploads

Upload the same photo to the Google Business Profile photo set and the Yelp photo set. Suggested caption for both:

> Sushi & Sashimi Combo, $35.

No other text is needed. The dish name and price are the point.

## 5. Server briefing

Brief the floor once at a pre-shift, then leave it alone for four weeks.

Who to offer it to: two-person tables, and guests who are clearly visiting the area or say they have not been in before.

What to say, in their own words:

> "If you would like a spread of both, the Sushi and Sashimi Combo is $35 and comes straight from the bar."

After the guest has eaten it, and only if the meal went well:

> "If you leave us a review, mentioning the fish helps other guests know what to order."

Do not offer anything in exchange for a review, and do not ask twice.

## 6. Four-week count

Count combos sold each week for four weeks starting the week you approve. One line per week, kept wherever you already track sales.

| Week | Combos sold | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | | |
| 2 | | |
| 3 | | |
| 4 | | |

At the end of week four, compare the four numbers. Rising or steady means keep the placement. Flat and low means the problem is the offer, not the photo, and we look at the price or the composition next.

# Direct Pickup Launch Plan (Draft — not live)

**Goal:** move takeout orders from commission marketplaces to your own Toast pickup page, so the same order earns more per ticket.

**Status:** draft for your approval. Nothing has been set up, posted, or printed.

---

## 1. Set up and test the Toast storefront (Day 1)

1. Open the Toast online ordering storefront for Harborview Japanese.
2. Load the takeout menu you actually want people ordering for pickup. If some items travel badly, leave them off.
3. Set pickup-only for now. Do not turn on delivery.
4. Place one real test order end to end: order a single item, pay, watch the ticket print in the kitchen, and pick it up. Confirm the receipt, the item name, and the pickup time all read correctly.
5. Refund or void the test order.
6. Copy the storefront link and keep it in one place. Every step below uses the same link.

**Before printing anything:** time three normal pickup orders during a weekday dinner. If they are not ready in 10–15 minutes, change the wording on the card and the phone script to the range you can actually hit.

---

## 2. Put the link where customers already look (Day 1–2)

Set the same Toast link as the ordering destination on:

- **Google Business Profile** — the "Order online" / Order button.
- **Yelp** — the ordering link on your business page.
- **Facebook** — the page action button (set it to "Order Now").
- **harborview.example.com** — a visible "Order Pickup" button on the home page.

After each one, click the live button from your phone and confirm it opens the Toast page, not a marketplace listing.

---

## 3. Bag card (draft copy)

Print a small card, roughly business-card or 3x5 size, single sided.

> **Order direct next time**
>
> Ready in 10–15 minutes
>
> [your Toast ordering link]
>
> Or call (555) 010-0000
>
> Harborview Japanese · 100 Harbor Point Dr, Harbor Point

Drop one card in **every** takeout and delivery bag for two weeks, including marketplace delivery bags. Keep the stack at the packing station so it becomes part of bagging, not a separate task.

---

## 4. Phone script for staff

When a caller asks how long the wait is, staff quote the time and then add one line:

# Restore ordering on harborview-order.example.com

**Status: draft for your review. Nothing here has been sent to anyone or changed on any website.**

## What we know
- Your main site is harborview.example.com.
- A separate ordering site, harborview-order.example.com, is showing a "temporarily not available" message instead of a working checkout.
- Phone and in-person are carrying orders that the site may be turning away.

## The order of work

**Step 1 - Today, during lunch service (5 minutes).**
On your own phone, off the restaurant wifi, open harborview-order.example.com and try to place a real order for pickup. Use the phone test script below. Stop at the payment screen only if you would rather not pay; note exactly where it blocked you.

**Step 2 - Today, right after the test.**
Find out who set up harborview-order.example.com. Likely candidates: the company that built your website, your point-of-sale provider, or a family member or former manager who registered it. Send them the message below and ask for an answer today.

**Step 3 - The one decision this creates.**
Once you know who controls the page, you pick one of two paths:

| Path | When it applies | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A. Keep it | harborview-order.example.com is still your intended ordering channel | Provider clears the banner and re-enables checkout today |
| B. Retire it | You have moved ordering to Toast or somewhere else | Its buttons and any links you control point to your current ordering page instead |

Do not leave it in the middle. A page that loads but refuses orders costs you more than a page that sends people straight to the right place.

**Step 4 - Verify for one week.**
Check the page once during lunch and once during dinner, every day for seven days, using the log below. Providers often restore a page and then have it revert after a system update.

**Step 5 - Count what you were losing.**
Ask staff to note any caller who mentions the website would not take their order. One week of tally marks tells you whether this page matters enough to keep.

## What I need back from you
After the phone test, tell me which path applies (A or B) and who controls the domain. If it is Path B, I will draft the exact link changes and a short note for anyone who still shares the old address.

# Weekday Lunch Bento Launch

**Status: draft on hold, nothing has been published.**

The plan is approved and ready to build. Before I can write the lunch menu, prepare the website section, or line up the photos, I need three facts from you. Everything else in the plan is already settled and does not need another decision.

## Already settled (no action needed from you)

- Photograph three bentos on the patio in daylight.
- Add a dedicated lunch section to harborview.example.com with those prices and photos.
- Upload the same lunch photos to the Google Business Profile and Yelp.
- Post the lunch menu as a Google Post once a week.
- Track midday covers separately for four weeks so we can tell whether this is working.

## What I need from you

1. **The lunch bento and special items with the prices you want shown publicly.** Exact wording as it should appear to customers, including any items you do not want listed online.
2. **Lunch days and service hours.** Which weekdays lunch runs and the start and end time.
3. **A shoot slot.** One weekday and time when the kitchen can plate three bentos for photos on the patio, plus which three bentos you want featured.

## What happens after you reply

Once I have those three answers I will send you, in one package for approval:

- The written lunch menu, formatted for the website and for Google Posts.
- A short shot list for the three patio photos.
- A simple midday cover tally sheet for the four-week tracking period.

Nothing goes on the website, Google, or Yelp until you approve that package.

## Why prices come first

Lunch pricing appears in three places at once: the website, the Google Business Profile, and Yelp. Correcting a wrong price across all three after the fact costs more time than confirming it now, and mismatched prices are the kind of thing guests mention in reviews. That is why the draft stops here rather than guessing.

# Weekday Lunch Bento — Draft Kit

Everything below is a draft for you to check. Nothing is live. **Confirm every price against your current till before anything goes on the website, Google, or Yelp.** Where I did not have a detail, there is a [square bracket] for you to fill in.

---

## 1. Lunch menu copy (with prices to confirm)

This is the text I would put on the website, on a printed card, and in the Google Post. Read it out loud once — if a phrase is not how you'd say it to someone at the counter, change it.

> ### Weekday Lunch
>
> Served [days, e.g. Monday to Friday], [start time] to [end time].
>
> Lunch is a bento: a main, rice, [side 1], [side 2], and miso soup, in one box. It comes out quickly, so it works if you have an hour.
>
> **Bento**
>
> - **[Bento name 1]** — [one short line: what the main is and how it's cooked] — $[price]
> - **[Bento name 2]** — [one short line] — $[price]
> - **[Bento name 3]** — [one short line] — $[price]
> - **[Bento name 4]** — [one short line] — $[price]
> - **[Bento name 5]** — [one short line] — $[price]
>
> **Lunch specials**
>
> - **[Special 1]** — [one short line] — $[price]
> - **[Special 2]** — [one short line] — $[price]
> - **[Special 3]** — [one short line] — $[price]
>
> **Add to any bento**
>
> - [Add-on, e.g. extra piece / side] — $[price]
> - [Add-on] — $[price]
> - [Drink, e.g. green tea] — $[price]
>
> Vegetarian: [name which bentos are vegetarian, or write "ask us and we'll put one together"].
>
> The patio is open at lunch when the weather allows. Takeaway available — [say whether you take phone orders and on what number, or delete this line].

**Notes for you before this goes live**

- Fill in the day range and hours exactly as they are now, not as they were.
- Every price above needs your eyes on it. If one is going up soon, put the new price in now rather than changing it in three weeks.
- If a bento is not available every weekday, either say which days or leave it off the printed list.
- Keep the descriptions to one line each. The photos do the rest of the work.

---

## 2. Photo plan — three bentos on the patio

The aim is three clear, honest photos that show what arrives at the table. Phone camera is fine.

**Which three:** pick your best-selling bento, one that looks most colourful, and one vegetarian or lighter option. Write them here so you don't second-guess it on the day:

1. [Bento] 
2. [Bento] 
3. [Bento]

**When:** a weekday before service, [suggest a time when the patio is in bright but indirect light — e.g. mid-morning]. Overcast is good. Avoid hard midday sun and avoid shooting into your own shadow.

**Setup:**

- One patio table, wiped down. Nothing else on it except the bento, chopsticks, and a cup of tea if you want it.
- Plate the box exactly as a customer receives it. No extra garnish that isn't normally there.
- Miso soup in shot beside the box, since it's included.

**Shots to get for each of the three (nine photos total, keep the best one or two of each):**

1. Straight down from above, the whole box filling most of the frame.
2. From about 45 degrees, so you can see depth in the compartments.
3. One wider shot with a bit of the patio visible — table edge, a chair, greenery — so people recognise where they'd be sitting.

**Practical points:**

- Shoot before the rice dries out or the tempura softens. Have the food come out and photograph it within a couple of minutes.
- Wipe any drips from the box edge.
- Tap the screen on the food to set focus and brightness. If it looks dark, brighten slightly; don't use a filter.
- Name the files something plain before uploading, e.g. `harborview-lunch-bento-[dish].jpg`.

---

## 3. Website — dedicated lunch section

Add a **Lunch** item to the main navigation, so it's one click from the homepage, not buried inside the dinner menu.

**Page structure:**

- **Heading:** Weekday Lunch
- **One line under it:** Served [days], [hours]. A main, rice, sides, and miso soup in one box.
- **The three photos**, side by side or stacked, near the top of the page.
- **The full menu text** from section 1, with prices.
- **At the bottom:** address, [phone number], and a line on whether lunch takes bookings or is walk-in only. [Fill in which.]

**Homepage:** add one line with a link, high enough that it's visible without scrolling — for example: *Weekday lunch bento, [hours]. See the lunch menu.*

**Check when it's up:** open the page on your phone. The prices should be readable without zooming, and the photos should load quickly.

---

## 4. Google Business Profile and Yelp

**Google Business Profile**

1. Upload the three lunch photos under Photos. Add the newest ones last so they sit near the front.
2. Check the hours listed match the lunch service you've just written down.
3. Under Products or Menu, add the bentos with their prices, or link to the new lunch page.

**Yelp**

1. Upload the same three photos.
2. Add a short caption to each: [Bento name], $[price], weekday lunch.
3. Update the menu link to point at the new lunch page.

---

## 5. Weekly Google Post — draft text

Post once a week, same day each week so it becomes a habit. Attach one of the three photos and rotate which one.

**Draft:**

> Weekday lunch at Harborview. Bento boxes from $[lowest price] — a main, rice, sides, and miso soup, served [hours], [days]. Patio open when the weather's good.
>
> This week's specials: [Special 1], [Special 2], [Special 3].

Each week, change only the specials line and the photo. Everything else can stay the same.

**A short version if the specials don't change:**

> Lunch is on [days], [hours]. Bento from $[lowest price] — main, rice, sides, miso soup. Eat on the patio or take it away.

---

## 6. Tracking midday covers for four weeks

Keep this simple enough that whoever is on the floor will actually do it. One sheet by the till, filled in at the end of lunch service.

| Week | Day | Lunch covers | Lunch takings | Weather | Notes |

**Notes column:** anything that explains an odd number — rain, a public holiday, roadworks, a large booking.

**Also worth writing down each week:** how many people mentioned seeing the lunch menu online. One tally mark is enough.

**At the end of four weeks, look at:** which bentos sold most, which days are quietest, and whether midday takings moved at all after the page went up. That tells you whether to keep the three photos or shoot the rest of the range.

---

## Your checklist

- [ ] Fill in days, hours, bento names, descriptions, and all prices
- [ ] Confirm every price against the till
- [ ] Decide which three bentos to photograph
- [ ] Take the photos on the patio
- [ ] Build the Lunch page and add it to the navigation

finds.title: Fix delivery value: add a fixed-price sushi set
finds.summary: Delivery reviewers are complaining about portion size for the price, so add one clearly-described fixed-price set and steer repeat orders to your commission-free Toast page.
finds.rationale: The delivery reviews split hard on value, not on taste: one guest paid $51 for three rolls and called it nowhere near the value, another paid $32 for a sushi sampler and was unhappy (390cc17d). Meanwhile the same listing shows a la carte rolls at $21.95 to $23.95 (91248c4e) and entrees from $23 to $54.95 (390cc17d), so a customer assembling an order has no way to feel they got a deal. A single named, photographed set at a fixed price with the piece count stated removes the guesswork and resets the value impression — this is the cheapest fix available because it is a menu-description change, not a discount. Your Toast page is commission free and money goes straight to you (91248c4e), so every order you move off the marketplaces is worth materially more per dollar than a delivery order.

# Draft: fixed-price sushi set for two

Everything below is a draft for you to review. Nothing is live anywhere. The set contents and price are blank in the places where only you can decide — fill those in and the rest is ready to go.

---

## 1. The set itself — for you to approve

Before anything else, fill in these three lines. Every other piece of this draft pulls from them.

**Set name:** Harborview Set for Two

**Contents:** [list exactly what goes in the box — e.g. X pieces nigiri, X pieces sashimi, X-piece roll, X-piece roll, plus sides]

**Total piece count:** [number] pieces

**Price:** $[price]

Two things worth checking before you sign off:

- The piece count in the description has to be the number that actually goes in the box, every time. If the count is awkward to hit consistently, change the count now rather than after it's listed.
- Price it against what two people currently spend when they order à la carte for delivery. If the set isn't clearly the better deal, it won't do the job it's meant to do.

---

## 2. Menu listing

This is the text for the top of the Toast ordering page and for the third-party menus. Same wording everywhere so the set reads the same no matter where someone finds it.

### Short version (for third-party platforms with tight character limits)

**Harborview Set for Two — $[price]**

[Number] pieces total: [contents, condensed — e.g. 12 pieces nigiri, 8 pieces sashimi, two 6-piece rolls]. Packed to travel.

### Full version (for Toast, where you have room)

**Harborview Set for Two — $[price]**

[Number] pieces total, made to order:

- [item — X pieces]
- [item — X pieces]
- [item — X pieces]
- [item — X pieces]
- [sides, e.g. ginger, wasabi, soy]

Enough for two people. Packed in one box so it arrives the way it left the kitchen.

### Placement notes

- **Toast:** put the set in the first position on the page, above [name of the section that currently sits at the top]. If Toast lets you pin a featured item, use that.
- **Third-party menus:** add the set to the top of the menu on each platform you're on — [platform], [platform], [platform]. Some platforms sort by their own logic; where you can't control position, at least make sure it sits in the first category a customer sees.
- Use the same photo everywhere (see below).

---

## 3. Photo brief

The point is that the photo shows what actually turns up at someone's door. No studio plate, no arrangement that the kitchen wouldn't send.

- Have the kitchen pack a real set, exactly as it would go out on a normal night. Don't let anyone tidy it up for the camera.
- Shoot it **in the open takeout box**, on the surface it would sit on — [counter or wherever makes sense].
- Shoot straight down from above. Fill the frame with the box. No props, no chopsticks laid across the corner, no extra garnish.
- Natural daylight if you can get it. Near [window or door] in the afternoon.
- Take one with the lid off and one with the lid partly on so the box is visible — the box being visible is part of the message.
- Count the pieces in the photo before you use it. If the photo shows more than the description says, the description is what people will hold you to.
- Reshoot if the set changes. A photo that's a piece count out of date does more harm than no photo.

---

## 4. Card for the delivery bags

One card in every bag, including the third-party orders. Suggested size: [postcard or business-card size — whatever your printer does cheaply].

### Front

**Order direct from Harborview**

[your Toast ordering URL]

Same kitchen, same food, no third-party fee on top.

[QR code to the Toast page]

### Back

**Harborview Set for Two — $[price]**

[Number] pieces. Enough for two.

[address]  
[phone]  
[hours]

### Notes

- Check the QR code with your own phone before you print a stack of them. Print a test of one first.
- Print [quantity] to start. If the cards move orders over to Toast, print more; if they don't, you've not spent much finding out.
- Ask whoever bags the orders to put a card in every bag, every time, not just the direct ones. Someone ordering through a platform is exactly the person you want to reach.

---

## 5. Two-week portion check

The risk with a set is that the box drifts — a piece short here, a smaller cut there — and the photo stops being true. Two weeks of checking builds the habit.

Print the photo and tape it up where the sets get packed. Then, for the first two weeks:

- Before each set goes in the bag, whoever packed it counts the pieces against the number in the description.
- Once a shift, put the packed box next to the printed photo and look at both. Does the box look like the picture? If not, note what's different.
- Keep a running note — a sheet on the wall is fine:

| Date | Sets out | Any short or off? | What was different |
|---|---|---|---|
| | | | |

At the end of two weeks, read the sheet. If the box matched the photo nearly every time, drop back to a spot check. If it didn't, the fix is usually one of two things: the piece count is unrealistic for a busy service, or the set needs a prep sheet by the station. Adjust the count and reshoot rather than letting the description stay wrong.

---

## Before this goes anywhere

1. Approve contents, piece count, and price.
2. Shoot the photo of the real packed box.
3. Fill the blanks into the menu text and the card.
4. Test the QR code, then print the cards.
5. Add the listing to Toast first, then the third-party menus.
6. Tape the photo up at the packing station and start the two-week sheet.

Send the filled-in contents and price back and I'll update the listing text, the card, and the photo brief so the piece count reads the same in all three.

# Ocean-View Patio Listing Refresh (Draft)

Nothing below has been published. Once you pick the wording, the updates can be made in one sitting.

The idea is simple: the patio and the ocean behind it are the first things a new guest should see and read, whether they land on the website, the Google listing, Yelp, or the Toast ordering page. Right now that has to be discovered. This puts it up front.

---

## 1. Homepage top line — pick one

This replaces the current top line of https://www.harborview.example.com/.

**Option A**
> Sushi on an ocean-view patio in Harbor Point.

**Option B**
> Fresh sushi, served on our patio above the Pacific.

**Option C**
> Come for the sushi, stay for the view from the patio.

Option A is the plainest and does the most work for search. Option B reads warmer. Option C is the most conversational. If none of them sound like you, write the line in your own words and it will be used as-is.

---

## 2. Google Business Profile description line — pick one

Add one sentence to the existing description. The rest of the description stays as it is.

**Option A**
> Our ocean-view terrace looks out over the water, with seating indoors as well.

**Option B**
> Guests can eat on the ocean-view terrace or inside, whichever suits the day.

---

## 3. Photo shot list

Six daylight photos, shot on a clear day. A recent phone camera is fine.

1. Wide shot of the patio with the ocean clearly behind it, no people in frame.
2. The same view with guests seated and the tables set.
3. A single table set for two, ocean in the background.
4. Close shot of a sushi order on a patio table, water visible behind it.
5. The patio as you first see it walking out from inside.
6. Late-afternoon shot with the light low over the water.

Avoid empty plates, stacked chairs, cloudy grey skies, and anything that crops the ocean out of frame. Shoot more than six and keep the best.

---

## 4. Where the photo and attributes go

- **Google Business Profile:** set the strongest patio photo as the primary image. Add the **Outdoor seating** and **Great view** attributes.
- **Yelp:** set the same photo as the first image in the gallery.
- **Toast ordering page:** set the same photo as the header or main image.
- **Website:** the new top line, with a patio photo beside or behind it.

Using the same photo everywhere is intentional. A guest who checks two listings before deciding should recognise the place both times.

---

## 5. What to check before anything goes live

- The homepage line and the Google description line are the ones you approved, word for word.
- No claim about hours, patio availability, or reservations has been added anywhere.
- The photos show the patio as it actually looks on a normal service day.
- The same image appears on Google, Yelp, and Toast.

---

**Next step:** reply with your chosen homepage line and description line, or send your own wording. The photos can be shot in the meantime.

## What this is

This is a draft for you to look over. Nothing has gone live yet — not the website, not Google, not Yelp, not the Toast page. Once you tell me which wording you like, all of it can be updated in one sitting.

The idea is simple: the patio and the ocean behind it are the best thing you have, and right now someone scrolling past your listings can't tell that's what they'd be walking into. Let's lead with it everywhere.

---

## 1. The line at the top of the homepage — pick one

Right now the first line doesn't mention the patio or the view. Here are three ways to say it. Keep it to one sentence so it still reads nicely on a phone.

**Option A — plain and clear**
> Sushi on an ocean-view patio in Harbor Point.

**Option B — a little warmer**
> Fresh sushi, served on our ocean-view patio above the Harbor Point coast.

**Option C — short and confident**
> Ocean-view patio dining. Sushi made to order.

One small thing: tell me the word you actually use for it — patio, terrace, or deck — and I'll use that same word in every place so nothing reads like it was written by different people.

---

## 2. One line added to your Google description

Nothing gets deleted here. This just gets added to what's already written:

> Harborview serves sushi from an ocean-view terrace overlooking the Harbor Point coastline.

If you'd rather say patio:

> Harborview serves sushi from an ocean-view patio overlooking the Harbor Point coastline.

---

## 3. Six daylight photos of the patio

A phone camera is fine. Pick a clear day, either mid-morning or about two hours before sunset — that's when the water looks best. Hold the phone level and sideways.

1. Wide shot of the whole patio with the ocean behind the tables.
2. One set table up close, ocean behind it, camera a little lower than usual.
3. A plate of sushi on a patio table with the water visible past it.
4. Two or three guests seated and enjoying themselves — ask them first.
5. The view itself, shot from where a seated guest's eyes would be.
6. The walk-up or entrance to the patio, so first-timers recognize it when they arrive.

Skip: harsh midday glare, cleared-but-not-wiped tables, service stations in frame, and any staff faces you haven't asked about.

---

## 4. Where each piece goes

| Place | Change |
| --- | --- |
| Google Business Profile | Best wide patio shot becomes the main image; other five uploaded |
| Yelp | Same shot set as the main image |
| Toast ordering page | Same shot as the header image |
| Google attributes | Turn on "Outdoor seating" and "Great view" |
| Website homepage | Top line replaced with the sentence you pick |

Using the same lead photo in all four spots matters more than it sounds like it does. Someone who spots you on Google and later lands on the Toast page should recognize it right away instead of wondering if it's the same restaurant.

---

## 5. What I need from you before anything is published

- Which homepage line you want, and which version of the Google description line.
- The word you prefer: patio, terrace, or deck.
- A yes on the six photos once they're shot — these become the first thing a new customer sees, so you should be happy with them.

Send those three back and I'll make the updates in one pass, then send the finished listings over for a quick look.

# Draft: leading with the ocean-view patio

Everything below is a draft for you to read, change, and approve. Nothing has been published or changed on any of your listings. Where I didn't have a fact, I've left it in [square brackets] for you to fill in.

---

## 1. Website homepage — new top line

This replaces whatever sits at the very top of the homepage now.

**Option A (recommended)**

> Harborview. [Cuisine — e.g. Japanese] cooking on an ocean-view patio in [town/neighbourhood].

**Option B — a little longer, if the space allows two lines**

> Harborview
>
> Our patio looks straight out over the ocean. Lunch, dinner, or a drink before the sun goes down.

**Option C — plainest**

> An ocean-view patio and a [cuisine] kitchen in [town/neighbourhood].

Pick one and I'd suggest keeping the same wording everywhere else on this page, so the patio is the first thing anyone reads no matter where they land.

If there's a second line under the headline, this works below any of the three:

> Open [days and hours]. Patio seating is [first come, first served / bookable at (link or phone)].

---

## 2. Photo brief — six daylight shots of the patio

A phone camera is fine. What matters is the light and that the ocean is clearly visible behind the tables. Best window is a clear morning or the hour or two before sunset — avoid harsh midday sun, which flattens the water and blows out the sky.

Before you shoot: wipe down the tables, straighten the chairs, clear the bins and any stacked crates out of frame, and set [one or two tables as you'd set them for service].

Shoot these six:

1. **The wide establishing shot.** Stand at the entrance to the patio, camera at chest height, so you get tables in the foreground and the ocean filling the top third of the frame. This is the one that will become your primary image.
2. **A set table with the ocean behind it.** Get low, close to the table, so the water sits just above the plates. No people needed.
3. **The view itself from a guest's seat.** Sit down at the best table and shoot what that person sees. Include a bit of the table edge or a glass in the corner so it reads as "from my seat," not a generic ocean photo.
4. **Food on the patio, ocean in the background.** One dish — [name the dish you want to lead with] — on a patio table, shot from slightly above, with the water soft in the background.
5. **The patio with people in it.** During a busy service, shot from behind or side-on so no one is identifiable close-up. Guests at tables, ocean behind. This is the one that makes it feel like somewhere people actually go.
6. **Golden hour.** Same angle as shot 1, taken 30–45 minutes before sunset. Keep this one for social and for the seasonal swap.

Shoot each one several times and pick the best later. Landscape orientation for all six — that's what Google and Yelp crop for.

---

## 3. Primary image changes

Once you've picked your favourite from shot 1:

- **Google Business Profile** — set it as the primary/cover photo, and upload the other five to the photo gallery.
- **Yelp** — set it as the primary photo.
- **Toast ordering page** — set it as the header image.

Use the same photo in all three places so anyone who sees you twice recognises you the second time.

---

## 4. Google Business Profile attributes to switch on

Under *Edit profile → Amenities / From the business*, tick:

- **Outdoor seating**
- **Great view**

These are the two that make you show up when someone filters for a view or a patio, so they're worth the two minutes.

---

## 5. Google Business description — line to add

Add this to the description you already have. It reads best as the opening line:

> Our ocean-view terrace is the heart of Harborview — every table on the patio looks out over the water.

**Alternative, if you'd rather it sat at the end:**

> Ask for the terrace when you arrive; every table out there looks straight out over the ocean.

---

## 6. Before anything goes live

Things for you to confirm or fix:

- Which homepage option — A, B or C?
- Fill in: [cuisine description], [town/neighbourhood], [days and hours], [whether the patio is bookable and how], [the dish for shot 4].
- Is "patio" or "terrace" the word you actually use with guests? I've used both above — worth settling on one and using it everywhere.
- Anything about the patio I should not promise — [heaters? covered in rain? closed in certain weather or months?]. If it closes in bad weather or off-season, we should not lead with it without a line saying so, or people will turn up disappointed.

Once you've marked up the wording and picked the photo, this is ready to go live.
